summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator lets mission planners compare lunar south-pole landing sites and dates in seconds. For any site, it computes the real terrain horizon from NASA LRO LOLA topography and traces the Sun and Earth across the sky with JPL ephemerides, including libration. The result shows exactly when a lander has sunlight for power and Earth in view for direct communications. Up to four sites can be compared side by side over the surface mission: percent sunlit, Earth in view, both together, longest darkness, longest Earth blackout, and time to sunset or Earthset at landing. A one-click scan shows how all of this changes if the landing slips at any time over the following year. Live shadow maps, a true-scale 3D terrain view with an eye-level camera, and playback show the result visually. A power budget turns it into battery and energy numbers. The geometry was validated against JPL Horizons (max error 0.0065°) and against NASA's published long-term illumination maps (mean difference 0.6 percentage points, r = 0.999).
details:
What it does. The challenge says that tools like Quickmap, Moon Trek and Horizons are powerful but slow when you need to compare scenarios quickly. Our app turns them into a single planner view:

- a south-pole map with NASA's average sunlight and Earth-visibility layers; click anywhere to add a site

- a sky view showing the terrain horizon and the Sun and Earth paths over the mission, drawn at true angular size and hidden by hills the way they really would be

- a mission timeline with Sun / Earth / both for each site

- a comparison table of the numbers engineers need for power, battery and comms decisions

- a "What if the landing slips?" scan: the share of the mission with both Sun and Earth, for every landing time across 12 months

- live shadows on the map within 30 km of the site, at any moment

- a Play button that animates the mission: the sky view, shadow map and 3D view move together

- a true-scale 3D terrain view lit by our shadow model, with an eye-level camera at the lander's mast

- a landing-window finder: every landing time in the next 12 months that keeps both Sun and Earth in view for the whole stay

- planner metrics: hours with the Sun up but Earth down, the longest total blackout, regional slope, and distance to the nearest permanently shadowed region (a water-ice science target, from NASA's PSR map)

- an at-a-glance KPI strip for the active site, and a mission-control styled interface that switches to solid panels for contrast

- a power budget from your own inputs (array output, load): sun-hours, energy, energy balance, and the battery needed for the longest night

- a mast-height slider showing how much a taller solar array or antenna gains over nearby terrain

- CSV export of the full time series, and shareable links, so science and engineering teams look at the same scenario.

How it works.

- Sun and Earth positions from JPL DE421 are expressed in the Moon's body-fixed MOON_ME frame, the same frame as the LOLA maps.

- For each site we trace 1,440 rays over LOLA 240 m topography and keep the highest terrain angle in each 0.5° of azimuth. Each sample is placed on the sphere in 3D, so lunar curvature is exact. There is no atmosphere, so there is no refraction.

- Visibility is computed every 10 minutes, including the partially visible solar disc.

- Live shadows apply the same rule to every map cell, tracing one ray toward the Sun along the curved surface, in a background Web Worker.

- Everything runs in the browser, with no server. A site is analysed in under a second, and the terrain download is 6 MB.

Validation. All the geometry is in one file, and the app and the validation script use that same code.

- Against the JPL Horizons API: 120 Sun/Earth positions at three sites, max error 0.0065°.

- Against NASA PGDA average Sun and Earth visibility maps (Mazarico et al. 2011, 18.6 years): 60 points beyond 85°S, randomly sampled within 5 illumination strata. Mean absolute difference was 0.58 and 0.53 percentage points; correlation was 0.999 and 0.998.

- Shadow map against the horizon method: 2,400 random point/time cases, 275 of them with the Sun within 1° of the terrain edge. There were zero lit/dark disagreements.

Benefits.

- When hardware delays or launch slips force a new landing date or site, planners can see within seconds whether the alternative still has power and a direct link to Earth, and for how long.

- The same view explains to students and the public why the lunar south pole is so hard: the Sun skims the horizon and Earth wobbles in and out of view.

Tools. Python (NumPy, Skyfield, Pillow) for the data pipeline; JavaScript (Canvas, Leaflet, three.js, Web Workers) for the app; Node.js for validation.

AI assistance. Some of Code, documentation and the demo deck were written with Anthropic's Claude (Claude Code) under the team's direction and review; this is also stated in the source file headers, the data files (si_note), the README and the app's "Data & validation" window.
